about: The parts of the ecosystem and the ideas a reader needs to work with it: Synapsis, platforms and dialects, kinds, the architecture of a project, results, the library, type definitions, contracts, plugins, generators, diagnostics, tests, the editors.

rows.title: What Synapsis is: the framework of NuclearLang
rows.summary: Synapsis is the framework built into the dialects: three platforms (`backend`, `mobile`, `web`), each written once in Nuclear. You write the business logic with kinds (`usecase`, `repository`, `controller`, a screen); the dialect writes the framework's code.
body: Writing an app usually means choosing and wiring many packages: state, JSON, dependency injection, HTTP, routing, translations, tests. With Synapsis the dialect already brings that architecture. In Nuclear you write only the business logic and the transpiler generates the rest.

- **Three platforms**: `backend` (HTTP APIs, data, events, AI agents), `mobile` (apps for Android, iOS, desktop and web) and `web` (web apps). A platform is what you write: its kinds, decorators, folders, `config.nuc`, plugins and tests.
- **Dialects** build a platform: `fastapi` and `nestjs` build `backend`, `flutter` builds `mobile`, `react` builds `web`. The Nuclear of a project never changes when its dialect changes.

- **The same way to think on every platform**: components by feature, kinds that say what a declaration is, one facade per component (`appcomponent`), errors as values (`Result`), connections listed in the configuration, tests written in Nuclear.
- **One CLI**: `nuclear new`, `gen`, `make`, `build`, `run`, `test`, `migrate`, `check`, `repair`, `explain`.
A new project: `nuclear new <name> -p backend` (or `-p mobile`, `-p web`; `-d` picks a dialect).

rows.title: Platforms and dialects: one code per platform, several technologies
rows.summary: A platform (`backend`, `mobile`, `web`) is what you write in Nuclear; a dialect (`fastapi`, `nestjs`, `flutter`, `react`) is only the language and framework the code comes out in. The Nuclear of a project never changes when its dialect changes.
body: | Platform | Dialects | What comes out |
| `backend` | `fastapi` (default), `nestjs` | a Python service or a TypeScript service |
| `mobile` | `flutter` | a Flutter app (Android, iOS, desktop, web) |
| `web` | `react` | a React web app |

- A platform is its kinds, decorators, folders, `config.nuc`, plugins and tests, identical for every dialect of that platform. Kinds and features may differ between platforms, never between the dialects of one platform.
- The project names both in `config.nuc`: `synapsis(platform = "backend", dialect = "fastapi")`. To move a backend to TypeScript, change `dialect` to `"nestjs"` and build: no other file changes.
- The only exception: code that uses a dialect's type definitions (a library that exists in one target only) is tied to that dialect.
- The standard library is Nuclear's own, so `xs.length` or `text.upper()` are written the same everywhere.
- The base language also has language dialects without a framework: `typescript`, `dart`, `python`.
An agent that writes a project names a platform, never a dialect: `nuclear check <file> --platform backend`.

rows.title: What a dialect is
rows.summary: A dialect is a folder of data (TOML files and templates) that tells the compiler how Nuclear is written in a target language or framework. It is loaded at run time, it can extend another dialect, and it is made without changing the compiler.
body: Like the adapter of an ORM: you write one form, and each dialect knows how to translate it to its technology.
- **Language dialects** write the base language in a target: `typescript`, `dart`, `python`.

- **Platform dialects** add a framework on top of a language: `fastapi` extends `python`, `nestjs` extends `nodejs` (which extends `typescript`), `flutter` extends `dart`, `react` extends `typescript`. They implement their platform's contract: its kinds, decorators and plugins.

- A dialect holds: the templates of each construct, its kinds and decorators, the imports each name needs, the standard library's translation, the project's files (manifest, entry point), its toolchain commands and the words the editor documents.
- The parser never changes for a dialect. Rust decides what is emitted; the dialect decides how.
List them: `nuclear dialect list`. For someone who writes a project a dialect is invisible: the project names a platform.

que es un dialecto

rows.title: Kinds: what a declaration is
rows.summary: A kind is the word that says what a declaration is (`usecase`, `repository`, `controller`, `entity`, `stateless`, `agent`). The dialect writes its class, decorators, registration and imports. Each platform has its native kinds; a project can add its own as a package.
body: A declaration starts with its kind, or gets it from its folder:
```nuclear
usecase FindCharacter(characters: CharacterRepository)
exec(name: string) Result<Error, Character>
~characters.byName(name)

- The kind decides where the file goes (`nuclear help layout --platform

`), which members it must or may have (a `usecase` has one `exec` that returns a `Result`), who may call it (the architecture rules) and what is generated for it.

- **Native kinds** belong to a platform: the backend has 16 (entity, repository, model, usecase, appcomponent, service, aggregate, controller, listener, tools, agent, state, graph, tests, appConfig, config); mobile and web have their own, with views and state managers.
- **Extension kinds** are packages (`kinds/<name>/`) written with TOML and templates on top of a dialect, never touching the compiler.

- Look one up instead of guessing: `nuclear help --platform

`; all of them: `nuclear help words --platform

`.
- `nuclear make <kind> <component> <Name>` writes the smallest file of a kind at its place.

rows.title: The architecture of a Synapsis project
rows.summary: A project is components by feature. Each component has its data (entities, repositories), its domain (models, use cases, services) and its entry points (a controller, a screen, an agent), and shows the rest of the app one facade: its `appcomponent`. The compiler enforces who may call whom.
body: ```text
config.nuc                      the platform, the dialect, the app, the plugins
config/project_config.nuc       appConfig: the connections (databases, an API, a model)
components/<feature>/
<feature>_appcomponent.nuc    the facade: aliases to the use cases (all the rest of the app sees)
data/                         entities and repositories
domain/                       models, use cases, services, aggregates
api/ | presentation/ | ai/    controllers (backend), screens (mobile, web), agents
test/                           the tests, in Nuclear
build/                          the generated project: never edited
The rules (the same idea on the three platforms):

- **One direction of calls.** An entry point (a controller, a state manager) calls the `appcomponent`; the `appcomponent` is only aliases to use cases; a use case calls repositories and services. A screen never calls a use case, a controller never calls a repository. A wrong call is `N0301`.
- **A component is closed.** Another component sees only its `appcomponent`, models and events, never its repositories or use cases (`N0302`).
- **One use case, one operation.** A `usecase` has one method `exec` that returns `Result<Error, T>`.
- **Dependencies are constructor parameters**, injected by type: `usecase CreateBook(books: BookRepository)`.
- **Connections are configuration.** A database, an HTTP API, a chat model, Kafka or Redis is listed in `appConfig`, never opened by hand.
- **Each file declares one thing** at the place its kind has in the layout, so anyone (a person, an agent, a generator) knows where everything is.
`nuclear check .` (or `nuclear check`) verifies all of it and writes the project map `.nuclear/map.md`: every declaration with its kind, its description and its members.

rows.title: The workspace: one business project and its apps (`.workspace/workspace.nuc`)
rows.summary: A workspace is a folder for one business project and the apps that form it (a backend, web sites, mobile apps), marked by `.workspace/workspace.nuc`. The editor, the MCP server and agents recognize it, so work starts there instead of searching a folder full of projects. `nuclear workspace` makes it and adds, renames and removes its apps; the MCP server does the same, asking the user first.
body: ```nuclear
// .workspace/workspace.nuc
workspace(name = "citofony", description = "An intercom for buildings")
app(folder = "citofony_api", platform = "backend")
app(folder = "citofony_web", platform = "web")
app(folder = "citofony_client", platform = "mobile")

- `nuclear workspace new <path> [--name] [--description]`, `add <app> --platform mobile|web|backend [--dialect]`, `remove <app> [--delete]`, `rename <app> <new>`, `edit`, `list`, `show`, `find` (all with `--json`); `--workspace <dir>`, else the workspace holding the current folder.

- Each app is a Synapsis project in its own folder of the workspace (its `config.nuc`); its folder is the snake_case project name. `nuclear new` run inside a workspace makes the app in the workspace's root and adds it.
- `nuclear check` in the workspace's root checks every app; `nuclear doctor` shows the workspace and a missing app's folder.
- An agent: `workspace_show` first, then `workspace_create` / `app_add` (never a loose folder); every change is asked first.
- The editor remembers the workspaces (recent ones) and shows the open one's apps as the projects of the Nuclear workspace.

rows.title: `config.nuc` and the connections: the configuration of a project
rows.summary: `config.nuc` at the root is the project's manifest in Nuclear: its platform and dialect, the app's name and version, the plugins it enables, the contracts it reads and its extra packages. The connections (a database, an API, a model) are listed in `config/project_config.nuc`.
body: ```nuclear
// config.nuc
synapsis(platform = "backend", dialect = "fastapi")
app(name = "tasks_api", description = "The tasks API", version = "0.1.0")
plugins(sqlite = true, ollama = true)
- `synapsis(platform, dialect)`: what the project is written for and what it is built with.
- `app(name, description, version)`: they reach the generated manifest.
- `plugins(...)`: the optional parts; a kind or a name of a plugin that is not enabled is `N0304`.
- `contracts(name = "../backend" | "https://...")`: a backend whose models and repositories are generated for this app (its contract also says its transports, guards and events).
- `dependencies(name = "version")`: extra packages of the target's package manager, written by `nuclear add <package>`; a name that is not an identifier is one text, `"date-fns@^4.4.0"`.
- `testEnv(NAME = "value")`: the environment the tests run with (a test token for a guard), set before the app is loaded.
The connections live in `config/project_config.nuc`, in the `appConfig`:
```nuclear
appConfig ProjectConfig
connections: Connection[] = [
SQLite(file = "app.sqlite", createTables = true),
Http(baseUrl = "https://rickandmortyapi.com/api"),

Real time and guards are configuration too: a backend's `WebSocketServer(path = "ws")` in `connections` and `guards: Guard[] = [NoOrigin(), Token(value = env("TOKEN"))]`; a web app's `WebSocket(url = "ws://...")` instead of `Http(...)` (can:real-time, can:backend-guards).

A value that changes per machine or per environment comes from `env("DATABASE_URL", "default")`, valued by the project's `.env` files and the keyring (concept:environments). A secret is never written in the code.
Several apps of one business project live in a workspace: a folder with `.workspace/workspace.nuc` that lists them, each with its own `config.nuc` (concept:workspace).

rows.title: Environments: `env()`, the `.env` files, the keyring and `--env`
rows.summary: A project of every platform reads a setting with `env("NAME", "default")` (no default: required). Values live in dotenv files beside `config.nuc` (`.env`, `.env.<environment>`, their `.local` versions ignored by git), secrets in the system's keyring; `--env <name>` on run, build, test and check picks one. Web and mobile get the values their code reads at build; a secret never reaches them.
body: ```nuclear
// config/project_config.nuc
appConfig ProjectConfig
connections: Connection[] = [Http(baseUrl = env("API_URL", "http://localhost:8000/"))]
guards: Guard[] = [Token(value = env("API_TOKEN"))]   // required: no default
- Precedence, lowest first: `.env` < `.env.<env>` < `.env.local` < `.env.<env>.local` < the keyring < the real process environment. `.env.local` is not read in `test`; `testEnv(...)` wins in tests.
- The environment: `--env <name>`, else `NUCLEAR_ENV`, else the active one (`nuclear env use <name>`, kept in `.nuclear/env`), else `development`; `nuclear test` uses `test`.

- `nuclear env list [--env e] [--json]`, `nuclear env set NAME value [--env e] [--local]`, `nuclear env set NAME --secret --env e` (the value from stdin, kept in the keyring; without one in `.env.<env>.local`), `nuclear env unset`, `nuclear env envs`, `nuclear env use e`. An agent uses the MCP tool `nuclear_env` (it never sets a secret: the user does, in a terminal).

- A backend: `nuclear run` passes the values to the app and refuses to start while a required one has no value (N0312 lists where it is used); `nuclear build --env e` writes the non-secret values into the app's `.env`, which the runtime loads without replacing the process's.

- Web and mobile: the build writes only the variables the code reads (`src/nuclear_env.ts`, `lib/nuclear_env.dart`); a secret read by a client is N0311. A name or default that is not a text literal is N0310.
- Every variable is listed in `.nuclear/contract.json` (`env`). In VS Code the Environments page (`Ctrl+Alt+Y`) edits them without opening a file.

rows.title: Errors are values: `Result<E, T>`
rows.summary: A function that can fail returns `Result<Error, T>` (the error type first): `Ok(value)` or `Err(error)`. Inside a function that returns a `Result`, a call to another one unwraps its value and returns its `Err` by itself; `match` handles both where it matters.
body: ```nuclear
usecase FindBook(books: BookRepository)
exec(id: int) Result<Error, Book>
book = ~books.find(id)          // an Err leaves the function here by itself
if not book.available
return Err(NotFound("book ${id} is not available"))
Ok(book)
- `Ok(v)` and `Err(e)` build a result; `x = f()` inside a function that returns `Result` gives the value and propagates the error. No `try`, no checks by hand.

- A `Result` is always handled; there is no way to discard it. Outside such a function (`N0108`): its error with `.error((e) => ...)` as a statement (`(~f(x)).error(...)` when `f` is async: `~` awaits the whole chain), with `match r` + `Ok(v) -> ...` / `Err(e) -> ...`, or kept and read (`isOk`, `value`, `error`); or the function returns `Result<E, ...>` so it propagates.
- An appcomponent's alias (`workspace() = GetWorkspace.exec`) gives the `Result` of the use case it names: `ws = workspaces.workspace(id)` in a use case is the value.
- The error propagates only when the error types are the same; convert it first otherwise (`N0109`).
- A backend controller answers the value of an `Ok`, or the status of the error: `NotFound` 404, `Invalid` 400, `Unauthorized` 401, `Forbidden` 403, `Conflict` 409.
- In a test, keep the result and read it: `found = ~books.byId(1)`, then `found.isOk`, `found.value.title`, `found.error.status`.
- `~` awaits an asynchronous call. A call used without it is `N0222`.
`try` / `catch e` / `throw` exist for the exceptions of libraries; business errors are results.
asks: how do I handle errors in nuclear

rows.title: The standard library is Nuclear's own
rows.summary: Strings, lists, maps, sets, numbers, dates, regex, bytes, `Math` and `Json` have one name per operation, the same in every dialect: `xs.length`, `xs.add(x)`, `text.upper()`, `x in xs`. A target's name (`push`, `len`, `toUpperCase`, `contains`) is error `N0114` with the Nuclear name as its fix.
body: - One name per operation. Properties without parentheses for cheap queries (`length`, `isEmpty`, `first`, `last`, `keys`, `values`); methods for the rest (`add`, `remove`, `map`, `filter`, `join`, `split`, `trim`, `replaceAll`).
- Membership is the operator `in`: `x in xs`, `"b" in text`, `key in map`. There is no `contains`, `includes` or `has`.
- Each dialect writes the target's expert code: `xs.length` becomes the target's own way to ask a length, with no runtime layer.
- The receiver's type decides the member. When the type of a value is not known, declare it: `items: string[] = ...` (`N0115`).
- A class of a library of the target (a UI widget, an HTTP client) is not part of the standard library: it is written as its type definition names it.
Look a member up: the rows `lib:string`, `lib:list`, `lib:map`... of this graph, or `nuclear help library`.

rows.title: Type definitions: the target's libraries, known to the compiler
rows.summary: A type definitions package describes the classes and members of a library of the target (like a `.d.ts`), per package and version. With it the compiler imports names by itself, completes them in the editor, and reports an invented class (`N0220`) or argument (`N0219`) with the closest real one.
body: - They are why an agent does not hallucinate APIs: a name that the definitions do not have is an error, with "did you mean".
- Imports are automatic: using a class of a library the dialect knows adds its import.
- Look instead of guessing: `nuclear defs show <Name> --dialect <d>` prints a declaration; `nuclear defs search <text> --dialect <d>` finds names; `nuclear defs list` lists the packages.

- A project gets the definitions of any package of its target with `nuclear add <package>` (`can:packages`); a backend or web project keeps them in `<project>/defs/`. Inside the project, `nuclear defs` shows them too.
- A name is imported as what it is: by name (`import { nanoid } from 'nanoid'`, `from tqdm import tqdm`), or as the package's default export (`import dayjs from 'dayjs'`).
- Code that uses a library of one target is tied to the dialect of that target.

rows.title: Contracts: one backend, its apps generated
rows.summary: A backend's build publishes what it exposes (`.nuclear/contract.json` and an OpenAPI document). An app declares it in `config.nuc` and gets its models and typed repositories generated at build time; a field the backend renamed breaks the app's build (`N0116`) instead of the app at run time.
body: 1. The backend builds: its contract is written in `.nuclear/contract.json` (models with their rules, controllers with their routes) and served at `/.nuclear/contract.json`.
2. The app declares it: `contracts(tasks_api = "../tasks_api")` (a folder) or a URL.
3. The app's build generates `contracts/<name>/`: the models and one repository per controller, ready to inject.
4. `nuclear contracts update` fetches a URL contract again; `nuclear contracts list` shows their state.
The same contract comes out whichever backend dialect built it. A contract that cannot be read is `N0307`.

rows.title: Plugins: only what the project uses
rows.summary: The optional parts of a platform (a database driver, Kafka, AI, a model provider) are plugins, enabled in `config.nuc` with `plugins(name = true)`. A project carries only the packages of the plugins it enables; using a kind or a name of one that is off is `N0304`.
body: - Backend: `sqlite`, `postgres`, `mysql`, `mariadb`, `redis`, `kafka`, `events`, `ai`, `openai`, `ollama`, `chroma`.
- Mobile: `genkit` and its providers `firebaseAI`, `googleAI`, `vertexAI`, `openAI`, `anthropic`.
- Web: none in this version.
- A provider enables what it needs (`ollama` enables `ai`).
- `N0304` says which line to add. Turning a plugin off removes its packages on the next build.
Each plugin has its row: `plugin:backend.ai`, `plugin:backend.sqlite`, `plugin:mobile.genkit`...

rows.title: Generators: the tools write the standard code, the agent writes what is special
rows.summary: `nuclear gen resource` writes the finished, compiling code of a resource from its data: the models, the repository, a use case per action, the facade, the controller or the screen, and the tests. An agent generates first and writes by hand only the logic no generator can know.
body: A feature such as "list the characters of an API, paged" is mostly code that follows from its data. That code is generated, not written by a model:
- `nuclear gen inspect`: what the project has (components, declarations by kind), so nothing is declared twice.
- `nuclear gen component <component>`: a component and its facade.

- `nuclear gen resource <component> <Name>`: everything of a resource. The fields come from `--fields "id:int name:string"`, from an example answer (`--from-json <file|url>`) or from a spec (`--from-spec spec.md`). `--source rest:<base url>` reads an API; `--source db` makes an entity and its queries (backend). `--actions list,get,search,create,update,delete` chooses the use cases. `--screen <screen>` adds a screen on mobile and web. `--dry-run` shows the files without writing them.

- `nuclear gen usecase <component> <Name>`: a use case wired into its component. The use case is one the project declares (its rules are written first; its signature is read from it): the command adds its alias to the facade and, on the backend, with `--route "POST orders/{id}/cancel"`, its route to the controller of `orders`. With `--calls <Repository>.<method>` the use case is written too, because all it does is call that method.
- `nuclear make <kind> <component> <Name>`: the smallest file of one kind.
Nothing is overwritten; a name declared elsewhere stops the generator before it writes. The templates belong to each platform, so the Nuclear a generator writes is the same for every dialect.

The same generators are MCP tools (`project_inspect`, `generate_component`, `generate_resource`, `generate_usecase`, `generate_screen`, `api_inspect`) and the first stage of the Builder. The order of work is always: inspect, generate, write only what is left, then wire it.
asks: how do I generate code with synapsis

sources: nuclear-synapsis-framework/docs/08-guides/README.md#Generators: the finished code of a resource

rows.title: Diagnostics: every error has a code, a place and usually its fix
rows.summary: The compiler reports each problem with a stable code (`N0114`), its line and column, a message and, when it is exact, the corrected text. `nuclear check --json` gives them to an agent, `nuclear fix` applies the exact fixes, and the errors shelf of this graph explains each one.
body: - Ranges: `N00xx` lexing and syntax, `N01xx` the resolver (names, results, the library), `N02xx` the dialect (kinds, decorators), `N03xx` the project and its architecture.
- The lexer and the parser never stop at the first error: all of them come back at once.
- A habit of another language (`await`, `const`, braces, `new`) is `N0022` with the Nuclear form.
- The cycle of an agent: write, `nuclear check --json`, apply `nuclear fix`, repair what is left with the message, check again until `[]`.
- One card per code: `error:N0114`, `error:N0222`... (`nuclear-graph card error:N0114`).
asks: what do the error codes mean
how do I fix a compiler error
how does nuclear report errors

rows.title: Tests are written in Nuclear, and first
rows.summary: A test is Nuclear too: `tests Name` with `@test("what it checks")` methods in `test/`, built for the target's test runner. `nuclear test` runs them. The work order is tests first: the test says what the code must do before the code exists.
body: ```nuclear
tests Books
@test("adds a book and finds it by its author")
addsAndFinds() void
books = inject<BooksAppComponent>()
made = ~books.add(NewBook(title = "Dune", author = "Herbert", year = 1965))
expect(made.isOk)
found = ~books.byAuthor("Herbert")
expect(found.value.length == 1)
- `inject<X>()` gives an instance; `~` awaits; `expect(condition)` checks.
- Backend: the databases are in memory and start empty in every test, so a test first creates the rows it reads. An agent's model is `FakeModel(["answer"])`.
- Mobile and web: `@mock([Repository])`, `@states(...)` for a state manager, `@widget(...)` for a screen.
- A failing test is explained at its `.nuc` lines by `nuclear explain`.
- A test that fails because of a bug in the code is reported, never deleted or weakened.

rows.title: The parts of the NuclearLang ecosystem
rows.summary: One repository, a project per folder: the language (compiler, language server, dialects), the framework Synapsis with its three platforms, the tools (the `nuclear` command, the code generator, the MCP server), the editor extensions and their tools, the devices, the Smart Graph, the roles and the local agents (on standby), Nuclear Chat, the installer and the website.
body: | Folder | What it is |
| `nuclearlang/` | the language: the compiler, the language server, the base words, the examples |
| `nuclearlang/dialects/` | the dialects: `python` (with `fastapi`), `typescript` (with `nestjs`, `react`), `dart` (with `flutter`), `nodejs` |
| `nuclear-synapsis-framework/` | the framework and its three platforms: `mobile`, `backend`, `web` |
| `tools/` | the `nuclear` command, the code generator, the MCP server (`nuclear-mcp`) |
| `extensions/` | the VS Code, JetBrains and Zed extensions and their tools (Nuclear Builder, HTTP Connections, Nuclear Atlas, the devices) |
| `device-emulators/` | the devices the tools and the editors start |
| `nuclear-graph-storage/` | the Smart Graph: the local, private knowledge base every agent reads |

| `nuclear-agents/` | the roles and skills every agent reads, and the local agents (the Nuclear Developer, on standby: ADR-platform-0013) |
| `nuclear-chat/` | Nuclear Chat, the software factory's workplace (a Synapsis backend and its embedded web UI), used by the Builder and Nuclear Atlas |
| `installer/` | the installers and the release |
| `website/` | the documentation site, written in Nuclear |
| `docs/` | what is about the whole platform: vision, architecture, decisions, standards |

How they fit: you write `.nuc`; one command, `nuclear`, checks and builds it and runs the project's life (new, make, gen, build, run, test); the editor shows it all through the language server; the graph knows everything written here; the agents and API providers you choose (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, OpenCode, Grok Build; an API model) reach the graph, the compiler and the generators through `nuclear-mcp`; the Builder takes a spec through a team of them; Nuclear Chat is where they answer you.
Each component's version has a row: `component:nuclear`, `component:nuclear-vscode`, `component:nuclear-graph`...

rows.title: The editors: VS Code, Android Studio (JetBrains) and Zed
rows.summary: One language server gives the three editors diagnostics, completion, hover, rename and the documentation of every word. VS Code adds the Nuclear workspace: run and debug `.nuc`, devices, HTTP Connections (an HTTP client), the Builder, Nuclear Atlas (the chat with the agent or API provider you choose, over the Smart Graph) and the settings of the AI pieces.
body: - **The language server** (`nuclear-lsp`): diagnostics with quick fixes, completion, hover with the documentation of a kind or decorator, signature help, rename. It follows the platform and dialect of the project's manifest (`config.nuc` or `nuclear.toml`).

- **VS Code** (`nuclear-vscode`): the Nuclear workspace with a tab per project and tools; the actions of the active project in the editor's title bar (run, debug, device, build, test, check); breakpoints in `.nuc` lines; the Synapsis device for a mobile app and a web device; HTTP Connections (`Ctrl+Alt+H`); the Builder (`Ctrl+Alt+P`); Nuclear Atlas, the chat with the agent or API provider you choose over the Smart Graph (`Ctrl+Alt+A`); the settings and integrations page (`Ctrl+Alt+S`).
- **Android Studio and IntelliJ** (`nuclear-jetbrains`): the language, `.nuc` breakpoints for a mobile app, and two tool windows: HTTP Connections (`Alt+Shift+H`) and Nuclear Builder (`Alt+Shift+P`).
- **Zed** (`nuclear-zed`): the language with a tree-sitter grammar and the same server, tasks and runnables.
The commands and shortcuts of VS Code are in the row `editor:vscode.commands`; its settings in `editor:vscode.settings.ai` and `editor:vscode.settings.editor`.

rows.title: NuclearLang is open source
rows.summary: Everything is open source under Apache-2.0, in one repository of the `nuclearlang` organization on GitHub: the language and its dialects, Synapsis and its platforms, the tools, the editor extensions, the Smart Graph, the Nuclear Developer (on standby) and the knowledge base.
body: - License: Apache-2.0 for the whole tree and every runtime package.

- Home: `https://github.com/nuclearlang/lang`, one repository; the website is `https://nuclearlang.github.io`; each folder is a project with its own `AGENTS.md` and `docs/`. The organization's profile is its own `.github` repository.

- A release is installed with one command: `curl -fsSL https://nuclearlang.github.io/install.sh | sh` (Linux, macOS) or `irm https://nuclearlang.github.io/install.ps1 | iex` (Windows). From the source tree: `installer/install.sh` (`--ai` also sets up the Smart Graph, the MCP server and Nuclear Chat).
